tasks: Reproduce the bug: seed 60 messages, fetch page 1 with OFFSET 0 LIMIT 20, insert one new message, then fetch OFFSET 20 LIMIT 20 and name the row that appears in both pages.
Rewrite getMessages in chat-app-api to use a (created_at, id) tuple cursor, and add a migration that widens idx_messages_channel_created to (channel_id, created_at DESC, id DESC).
Add encodeCursor and decodeCursor helpers with a zod schema on the decode path, then send a tampered cursor and confirm the API returns 400, not 500.
Fetch limit + 1 rows and return { items, nextCursor }; assert nextCursor is null on the final page and non-null on every other page.
Insert two messages inside a tight loop so they share a timestamp, then page through with a timestamp-only cursor and prove one message is unreachable.
Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the offset query at OFFSET 40000 and on the keyset equivalent; write down rows-scanned and timing for both.

quiz.q: An infinite-scroll feed backed by OFFSET pagination shows the same post twice. What is the actual cause?
options: The client appends results without deduplicating by id
Rows shift position when new rows are inserted, so the next OFFSET window overlaps the previous page
Postgres returns rows in non-deterministic order when there is no primary key
The connection pool returned a cached result set
quiz.explain: OFFSET addresses a position in the result set. An insert above the window pushes every row down one, so the row at the page boundary lands inside the next page too. Client-side dedupe hides the symptom without fixing the pagination.

quiz.q: Why does the cursor carry id alongside created_at?
options: So the client can sort locally
Because created_at is not indexed on its own
Because two rows can share a created_at, and a non-unique boundary silently drops or repeats rows
Because UUIDs happen to sort chronologically
quiz.explain: Keyset pagination needs an unambiguous 'the row after this one'. If two rows compare equal on the sort key, the boundary is undefined and rows fall through the crack with no error.

quiz.q: What does DESC buy you in the index (channel_id, created_at DESC, id DESC)?
options: A physically smaller index
Postgres can read the index forward for a newest-first query instead of walking it backward
Faster inserts, because new rows land at the end
It forces an index-only scan
quiz.explain: B-tree indexes are ordered. Matching the index direction to the query's ORDER BY lets Postgres scan forward, which is measurably cheaper than a backward scan at scale.

quiz.q: When is OFFSET still the right tool?
options: A chat message list
An admin table over mostly-static data that genuinely needs numbered pages
Any activity feed with live inserts
Any endpoint the mobile app calls
quiz.explain: Keysets cannot jump to page 7. When numbered pages are a real product requirement and the data is not being written under the reader, offset is fine — just cap how deep it can go.

quiz.q: The API returns nextCursor: null. What should the client do?
options: Stop requesting; it has reached the end of the list
Retry with the previous cursor
Fall back to offset pagination
Re-request the first page to refresh
quiz.explain: A null nextCursor is the end-of-list signal. That is the whole contract, which is why you don't also need a total count or a hasNextPage flag that could disagree with it.

tasks: Read src/services/realtime.service.ts end to end, then draw the path from POST to the other device's re-render, naming every hop including the WAL.
Connect two wscat clients with valid tokens, join the same channel, POST a message with curl, and confirm both sockets receive it without either one polling.
In a scratch database, skip ALTER PUBLICATION supabase_realtime ADD TABLE messages and confirm POST still returns 201 while no socket event arrives.
Drop one client's connection for 30 seconds, POST from the other, reconnect, and prove the missed message only appears after a fetch-since-cursor.
Add a ping/pong heartbeat plus client reconnect with exponential backoff, and verify a 60-second idle connection survives.
Map payload.new into an explicit response shape before broadcasting instead of forwarding the raw row, and note which columns you chose to withhold.

quiz.q: Which HTTP status code completes a WebSocket handshake?
options: 200 OK
101 Switching Protocols
204 No Content
426 Upgrade Required
quiz.explain: The client sends an ordinary GET with Connection: Upgrade, and the server answers 101. The TCP connection is not reopened — it stops speaking HTTP and starts carrying WebSocket frames.

quiz.q: Why write over REST and only receive over WebSocket, rather than sending messages up the socket?
options: WebSocket frames cannot carry JSON
The POST path gives you auth, validation, rate limiting, transactions and a real error response, and the committed row is the fact the socket merely announces
Supabase Realtime cannot observe writes made over a socket
Sockets are slower than HTTP for writes
quiz.explain: The socket has no middleware stack and no way to return a structured error. Keeping writes on REST means the database stays the source of truth and the socket is only a notification channel.

quiz.q: Why does the client still need a fetch-since-cursor when a socket reconnects?
options: To refresh the auth token
Because events that occurred while the socket was down are never replayed, so the gap can only be closed from the database
Because Realtime replays missed events, so this is just belt-and-braces
To re-register presence
quiz.explain: Realtime is a live stream, not a log you can rewind. Anything that happened during the disconnect is gone from the socket's perspective and has to be read from Postgres.

quiz.q: When is SSE the better choice than a WebSocket?
options: When the client needs to push typing events upstream
When only the server pushes — notifications, counters — and you want plain HTTP semantics every proxy understands
When you need to send binary frames
When you run more than one server instance
quiz.explain: SSE is a long-lived HTTP response. If the client never needs to talk back, it gives you server push with none of the upgrade, framing, or proxy-compatibility work.

quiz.q: Why one global postgres_changes subscription with server-side fan-out instead of one subscription per channel?
options: Per-channel subscriptions cannot filter by event type
Subscription count would scale with active channels and hit service limits, while fan-out from one subscription keeps it at one
Global subscriptions are more secure
Postgres supports only one publication per database
quiz.explain: A thousand active channels would mean a thousand subscriptions. One subscription plus a channel-to-sockets map delivers the same events with constant subscription cost.

tasks: Replace any boolean online flag with a map of userId to a set of sockets, and broadcast only on the first connect and the last disconnect.
Open two wscat connections as the same user, close one, and confirm no offline event is broadcast; close the second and confirm exactly one is.
Implement the typing TTL, then kill a client mid-typing and confirm the indicator clears within the TTL instead of sticking.
Add the token-bucket middleware to the send-message route with capacity 20 and refill 2/s, hammer it in a loop, and confirm a 429 with a Retry-After header.
Restart the server and show that in-memory buckets reset to full; write down what you would change to run three instances safely.
Read the bucket cleanup interval in chat-app-api and estimate how much memory the map would hold after a month without it.

quiz.q: Why is a users.is_online boolean column the wrong model?
options: Booleans cannot be indexed in Postgres
It cannot represent multiple simultaneous connections, and nothing resets it when the process dies
Writing it on every connect is too slow
Row-level security cannot protect a boolean
quiz.explain: Online is derived from live sockets. Storing it as a fact creates a second source of truth that drifts on a second device, a crash, or a deploy.

quiz.q: A user is connected on phone and laptop. The laptop tab closes. What should the server broadcast?
options: Nothing — the user still has a live connection and stays online
An offline event, then an online event when the phone next sends anything
An offline event, because one connection closed
A presence event with a connection count
quiz.explain: Presence is a reference count. Offline is broadcast only when the set of that user's sockets becomes empty.

quiz.q: Why does the typing indicator rely on a TTL instead of an explicit stop message?
options: Because a stop message is bigger on the wire
Because users do not explicitly stop typing, and a stop frame that never arrives leaves the indicator stuck forever
Because timers are cheaper than broadcasts
Because the client cannot detect blur events
quiz.explain: People trail off, background the app, or lose signal. A TTL bounds the worst case at a slightly late clear rather than a permanent lie.

quiz.q: Token bucket versus a fixed 'N per minute' counter — what does the bucket give you?
options: Lower memory usage
A bounded burst for real usage while still holding a long-run average rate
Protection against distributed attacks
Per-endpoint limits instead of per-user limits
quiz.explain: A counter permits the entire allowance in the first second and then blocks. Capacity plus refill rate expresses burst and ceiling as two independent numbers.

quiz.q: You run three API instances with in-memory buckets and a limit of 20 requests per second per user. What is the effective limit?
options: 20 per second, the load balancer keeps a user on one instance
About 60 per second, because each instance keeps its own bucket
7 per second, because the limit is divided
Unlimited, because the buckets never sync
quiz.explain: Local state means one bucket per instance per user. Shared limits need shared storage — that is the moment Redis stops being optional.

tasks: Move thumbnail generation out of the upload route into a job, and record the endpoint's response time before and after.
Split the worker into its own entrypoint src/jobs/worker.ts with a dev:worker script, and remove the workers import from server.ts.
Configure attempts: 3 with exponential backoff, make the handler throw on purpose, and write down the actual retry timestamps you observe.
Validate job.data with a zod schema at the top of every handler, then enqueue a malformed payload and confirm the job fails without killing the worker.
Write an idempotent handler for a notification job using a unique constraint as the dedupe key, and run the same job twice to prove one send.
Add an authenticated queue-depth endpoint returning waiting, active and failed counts for all three queues.
Do both halves of the trap below and write one sentence on how you would have detected each in production.

quiz.q: Which of these belongs inside the request path?
options: Resizing the uploaded image into three sizes
Writing the database row the user asked you to create
Sending the push notification to the recipient's device
Recomputing the account's aggregate storage total
quiz.explain: The user is waiting for the thing they asked for. Slow work, third-party calls, and derived aggregates all belong on the other side of a queue.

quiz.q: BullMQ retries give you at-least-once delivery. What does that require of your handlers?
options: They must complete within the visibility timeout
They must be idempotent, so running the same job twice has the same effect as running it once
They must never throw
They must run with concurrency 1
quiz.explain: A worker can die after doing the work but before acking it. Overwriting the same thumbnail path is naturally safe; sending an email is not, so the handler needs its own dedupe key.

quiz.q: Why exponential backoff rather than retrying immediately?
options: It reduces Redis memory usage
Failures are usually temporary, and instant retries pile more load onto the thing that is already struggling
BullMQ requires a delay between attempts
It guarantees the job eventually succeeds
quiz.explain: 5s, 25s, 125s gives an overloaded dependency room to recover. A tight retry loop turns a brief outage into a sustained one.

quiz.q: You enqueue to a queue name no worker was constructed for. What happens?
options: add() rejects and the request returns 500
BullMQ logs a warning and drops the job
add() resolves with a job id, the request returns 201, and the job waits in Redis forever with nothing logged
The job is delivered to the closest matching queue
quiz.explain: Producing and consuming are decoupled by design, so nothing on the API side can tell the difference. Queue depth is the only place this shows up.

quiz.q: What does concurrency on a Worker control?
options: How many worker processes BullMQ starts
How many jobs that one worker instance processes simultaneously
How many retry attempts run in parallel
How many Redis connections the queue opens
quiz.explain: It is a per-worker parallelism budget. For CPU-bound work like sharp, keep it low — two to four — or the box becomes unresponsive.

trap.title: Two ways a job silently never runs
trap.content:
Both of these produce a successful API response, no error log, no crash, and no job. Do them on purpose, today, in `file-vault-api`.

**Failure 1 — nobody is listening.**

In the upload route, change the producer's queue name to something no worker constructs:

```ts
await new Queue("thumbnails", { connection: redis }).add("generate", {
  fileId: file.id,
  storagePath: file.storage_path,
});
// note the trailing "s" — the worker listens on "thumbnail"
```

Upload an image. You get a 201. `add()` resolved with a real job id. Redis is faithfully holding a job in a list that no `Worker` will ever read. Then check the queue you thought you used:

```ts
await thumbnailQueue.getWaitingCount(); // 0 — the right queue is empty
```

The job is real, durable, and orphaned. Nothing in your logs mentions it, because nothing went wrong. The same thing happens if you typo the *worker's* name instead, or add a fourth queue and forget to construct its worker, or deploy the API without deploying the worker.

**Failure 2 — the worker isn't running.**

Stop the worker process. Leave the API up. Upload five images. Every request returns 201 in about 200ms — faster than usual, because nothing is competing for CPU. The app looks perfect. Then look at the rail:

```bash
redis-cli LLEN bull:thumbnail:wait   # 5
```

Start the worker and watch all five fire at once. Now imagine that gap was a long weekend, the queue holds forty thousand jobs, and the first thing your freshly deployed worker does is attempt all of them.

**What both prove.** The API cannot distinguish "the job ran" from "the job will never run," because it never knew either way. The only honest signal lives on the queue: waiting count, failed count, the age of the oldest waiting job, and whether a worker has checked in recently. Add an authenticated `GET /admin/queues` that returns `getWaitingCount()`, `getActiveCount()`, and `getFailedCount()` for each queue. Look at it after every deploy, and alert when waiting count stays above a threshold for more than a few minutes. It's the cheapest observability you will ever build, and the reason to build it is that you have now seen both silences yourself.

tasks: Trace one upload through upload.ts, files.ts and file.service.ts, and write out the stations in the order they actually execute.
Move the quota check as early as you can, return 413 with used_bytes and quota_bytes, and note what stops you from checking before any bytes arrive.
Add magic-byte sniffing for images and reject an executable renamed to .jpg; confirm the response is a 400 that names the real problem.
Handle MulterError LIMIT_FILE_SIZE explicitly so an oversized file returns 413 instead of a generic 500.
Delete the compensating storage remove, force the DB insert to fail, then find the orphan object in the bucket and put the remove back.
Make the bucket public briefly, fetch a file with no auth header, then set it private and confirm the same URL fails; write down what that proves about unguessable URLs.
Return file ids from the API and mint signed URLs on demand; cache one for an hour and watch it expire.

quiz.q: Why upload the bytes to storage before inserting the database row?
options: Storage is slower, so starting it first overlaps the work
The row needs the storage path, and an orphan object is a cheaper problem than a row pointing at nothing
Supabase requires the object to exist before an insert
It lets you skip the quota check
quiz.explain: There is no transaction across storage and Postgres. Order the steps so the failure you can end up with is the one you can clean up, and write the compensating delete for it.

quiz.q: Why is the storage path a generated UUID instead of the client's filename?
options: UUIDs compress better
It removes path traversal, collisions and encoding problems in one move, and the real name still lives in the row
Supabase Storage rejects filenames with spaces
It makes the file unguessable, which is the access control
quiz.explain: Anything client-supplied is a claim. Deriving the path server-side turns a malicious or awkward filename into a harmless UUID while the display name stays in the database.

quiz.q: What does a signed URL actually contain?
options: An encrypted copy of the file path
The path, an expiry, and an HMAC over both — so tampering breaks the signature and time breaks the URL
A one-time token stored in the database
The user's JWT
quiz.explain: The signature is what makes it unforgeable and the expiry is what makes it temporary. It is the same construction as an S3 presigned URL.

quiz.q: Why is a public bucket with UUID filenames not access control?
options: UUIDs can be brute-forced quickly
There is no expiry, no revocation, no per-user check and no audit trail, and URLs leak through logs, analytics and screenshots
Public buckets are slower
Supabase charges more for public egress
quiz.explain: Obscurity gives you no ability to say no later. A private bucket plus short-lived signed URLs puts your own authorization code on the path every time.

quiz.q: When would you choose multer's diskStorage over memoryStorage?
options: When forwarding straight to cloud storage
For large files, or when a tool needs a real file on disk — accepting that you now own the cleanup
When you need MIME validation
When the client sends multiple files
quiz.explain: memoryStorage is right when the buffer's next stop is an upload call. Multi-gigabyte files or shell tools like ffmpeg need a path on disk, and temp files you must delete.

m3-6.content:
## The problem

Three screens in the file vault, three self-inflicted wounds.

**The folder tree.** You fetched the root folders, then for each root its children, then for each of those theirs — one request per node. Four levels deep and forty folders, and the sidebar takes six seconds on hotel Wi-Fi. You've written this loop in a React Native app and blamed the network.

**The metadata.** Images need width and height. PDFs need a page count. Videos need duration and codec. You added five nullable columns, then a sixth, and now every migration adds a column that's NULL for 95% of rows and a `?.` in every consumer.

**The usage bar.** `GET /usage` runs `SELECT COUNT(*), SUM(size_bytes) FROM files WHERE user_id = $1`. Instant at 200 files. At 200,000 it's 900ms, it runs on every screen open, and it's the slowest query in your logs — to render a progress bar nobody reads to the byte.

## The idea

Three Postgres features with intimidating names and small ideas underneath.

**Recursive CTE** — a loop whose queue is a result set. Start with a row, find its children, find *their* children, stop when a pass returns nothing. It's the tree traversal you were writing in JavaScript, moved to where the data already lives, so it costs one round trip instead of forty.

**JSONB** — a `Record<string, unknown>` column that Postgres actually understands. Stored as a parsed binary structure, so you can read inside it, filter on it, and index it. Use it for fields that genuinely differ from row to row.

**Materialized view** — a memoized selector with manual invalidation. A regular view is a saved *query*, re-run on every read. A materialized view is a saved *answer*, stored as a real table, recomputed when you say so. You trade freshness for a lookup that costs the same at 200 rows and 200,000.

## In practice

The tree, in one query. `folders.parent_folder_id` references `folders.id` — a self-referential foreign key, which is all a tree is.

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE folder_tree AS (
  -- base case: where to start
  SELECT f.id, f.parent_folder_id, f.name, f.path, 0 AS depth
  FROM folders f
  WHERE f.user_id = $1 AND f.id = $2

  UNION ALL

  -- recursive case: children of whatever the previous pass found
  SELECT f.id, f.parent_folder_id, f.name, f.path, ft.depth + 1
  FROM folders f
  JOIN folder_tree ft ON f.parent_folder_id = ft.id
  WHERE f.user_id = $1
)
SELECT * FROM folder_tree ORDER BY path;
```

It runs in passes. Pass 0 finds `Documents`. Pass 1 joins against pass 0's rows and finds `Work` and `Personal`. Pass 2 finds `Reports` and `Invoices`. Pass 3 finds nothing, so it stops. `depth` comes along free and gives the client its indentation.

Note `user_id = $1` in *both* halves. An ownership filter that appears only in the base case is an authorization hole — the recursion walks straight into someone else's rows the moment a `parent_folder_id` crosses accounts.

JSONB, for metadata that differs by file type:

```sql
metadata jsonb NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'
```

```sql
-- read a field: ->> returns text, -> returns jsonb
SELECT metadata->>'thumbnail_path' FROM files WHERE id = $1;

-- merge, without clobbering the other keys
UPDATE files SET metadata = metadata || '{"thumbnail_path":"x/y_thumb.jpg"}'::jsonb
WHERE id = $1;

-- only once you genuinely filter on it
CREATE INDEX idx_files_metadata ON files USING GIN (metadata);
```

The rule: **JSONB is for data you don't query on structurally.** The moment a field shows up in a `WHERE` on a hot path, or wants a `NOT NULL`, a foreign key, or a `CHECK`, it wants to be a column. `size_bytes` is a column — you sum it, you enforce a quota with it. `codec` is JSONB — you display it. And if you do filter inside JSONB, index it: a GIN index makes containment queries like `metadata @> '{"codec":"h264"}'` fast, where a B-tree can't help at all.

The usage bar, precomputed:

```sql
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW user_storage_usage AS
SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS file_count, COALESCE(SUM(size_bytes), 0) AS total_bytes
FROM files
GROUP BY user_id;

-- required for CONCURRENTLY, and it makes the read a single index hit
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_user_storage_usage_user ON user_storage_usage(user_id);
```

Reads become `SELECT * FROM user_storage_usage WHERE user_id = $1`: one row, one index lookup, the same cost at any table size. The catch is that it's wrong the instant anyone uploads anything. So you refresh it:

```sql
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY user_storage_usage;
```

`CONCURRENTLY` builds the new copy alongside the old one and swaps them, so readers are never blocked — which is exactly why the unique index is mandatory. Refresh from a job after uploads and deletes, or on a schedule with pg_cron. Either way you have chosen to be a little bit wrong, on purpose, in exchange for a screen that loads. That's what **stale by design** means, and it's only acceptable when being slightly wrong is harmless.

## In your world

All three live in `file-vault-api`: `get_folder_tree()` in the migration, `files.metadata` on every uploaded file, and `user_storage_usage` behind `getStorageUsage()`. Work to do: add a cycle guard to the recursive CTE, add the GIN index plus a query that uses it, then break the view on purpose — set `STORAGE_QUOTA_MB` tiny, upload past the quota *without* refreshing, and watch the quota check wave you through. That's exactly the bug you'd ship by using a materialized view as an enforcement mechanism.

Your work backend precomputes feed data in background jobs for the same reason: some answers are too expensive to compute per request, so they're computed on a schedule and served slightly stale. Different table, identical bargain — and the same question to ask before you accept it: what breaks if this number is thirty seconds out of date?

## Watch out

- **A recursive CTE with a cycle never terminates.** If a folder ever becomes its own ancestor — a bad move, a bad import — the query runs until something kills it. Carry visited ids in an array and add `WHERE NOT f.id = ANY(ft.visited)`, or cap `depth`.
- **JSONB has no constraints.** No foreign keys, no NOT NULL, no type checking. `{"widht": 1920}` is a perfectly valid write, and you find out three weeks later when no thumbnail has a width.
- **`metadata->>'width' > '1000'` compares strings.** `'900' > '1000'` is true. Cast it: `(metadata->>'width')::int > 1000`.
- **Never enforce a hard limit from a materialized view.** Quotas that must not be exceeded, balances, anything billable — those need a live count or a trigger-maintained counter. The view is for the progress bar, not the gate.
- **`REFRESH` recomputes everything.** It's a full scan and aggregate. Refreshing after every single upload on a busy system costs more than the query you were avoiding, so debounce it.

## Checkpoint

Six questions. Out loud, no notes, no editor open.

1. Draw twenty feed rows. Someone posts while the user is reading page 1, then the client asks for page 2 with `OFFSET 20`. Which row does the user see twice, and why? Now show me what the keyset version sends instead — and why the cursor is `(created_at, id)` and not just `created_at`.
2. Why is the worker a separate process? Name a failure that separation prevents, and one it does not.
3. Give me two ways an enqueued job silently never runs. For each: what signal would have told you, and where would you have had to look for it?
4. When is JSONB the wrong choice? Point at a specific field in the file vault you'd refuse to put in `metadata`, and say what you'd lose by putting it there.
5. `user_storage_usage` is stale by design. Explain the phrase, then name one thing you must never enforce with it and what you'd use instead.
6. A message is delivered over the socket, but the database write failed. Which is the source of truth, what should the other client be showing, and what makes it correct again?
tasks: Replace the per-node folder fetch with one get_folder_tree() RPC call and count the round trips saved on a four-level tree.
Add a cycle guard to the recursive CTE, then create a cycle with a manual UPDATE in a scratch database and confirm the guarded query still terminates.
Repeat the user_id filter in both halves of the CTE, then remove it from the recursive half and demonstrate the rows it lets through.
Add the GIN index on files.metadata, write a containment query that uses it, and compare EXPLAIN output before and after.
Find and fix a string-comparison bug: compare metadata->>'width' as text versus cast to int and show the differing results.
Set STORAGE_QUOTA_MB tiny, upload past the quota without refreshing the materialized view, and document exactly how far over you got.
Refresh the view from the storage-quota job, then drop the unique index and confirm REFRESH CONCURRENTLY fails.
Answer all six checkpoint questions out loud with no notes, and write down the ones you fumbled.

quiz.q: How does a recursive CTE know when to stop?
options: At a fixed recursion depth set by Postgres
When a pass returns no new rows
When the base case is exhausted
When it reaches the LIMIT
quiz.explain: Each pass joins against the previous pass's output. An empty pass ends the recursion — which is also why a cycle never terminates without a guard.

quiz.q: Which field belongs in a real column rather than in a JSONB metadata blob?
options: A photo's EXIF camera model
size_bytes, because you sum it, index it and enforce a quota with it
A video's codec name
A PDF's page count
quiz.explain: JSONB is for data you don't query on structurally. The moment a field needs NOT NULL, a foreign key, a CHECK, or a fast filter on a hot path, it wants to be a column.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a view and a materialized view?
options: A view can be indexed; a materialized view cannot
A view is a saved query re-run on every read; a materialized view is a stored answer that only changes when you refresh it
A materialized view updates automatically when the underlying rows change
A view is read-only; a materialized view is writable
quiz.explain: That stored answer is why reads are a single index lookup at any table size, and also why it is wrong the moment the underlying data changes.

quiz.q: REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY requires what, and why?
options: A unique index on the view, so the new copy can be built alongside the old and swapped without blocking readers
An exclusive lock taken in advance
pg_cron to be installed
The view to contain no aggregates
quiz.explain: Without CONCURRENTLY the refresh locks the view and reads stall. With it, Postgres needs the unique index to match old rows to new ones during the swap.

quiz.q: What does 'stale by design' mean for user_storage_usage?
options: The view is deprecated and should be replaced
It is knowingly a little out of date between refreshes, which is fine for a progress bar and unacceptable as a hard quota gate
It refreshes lazily on first read after a write
It caches only rows that were read recently
quiz.explain: You traded accuracy for a constant-cost read. That trade only holds where being slightly wrong is harmless — never for enforcement, balances, or anything billable.

sq-3.content:
## The problem

Every chat app opens on the same screen: a list of conversations, each showing its last message and an unread badge. It looks trivial. It's the hardest query in the product. Fetch the channels, then for each one fetch the newest message, then for each one count the unread — twelve conversations becomes twenty-five queries, and the screen everyone sees first is the slowest one you have.

## The idea

"For each row in this set, run this small query" has a name in SQL: `LATERAL`. A normal subquery can't see the outer row. A lateral subquery can, which makes it a `for` loop that runs inside Postgres, using indexes, in one pass — the exact thing you'd otherwise write as `channels.map(...)` with a round trip inside the callback.

Put that query in a **stored function** and the whole screen becomes one call. Read receipts get the matching treatment: an UPSERT, which is one atomic statement instead of a check-then-write race.

## In practice

The shape to internalize, from `get_user_channels()` in the migration:

```sql
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT m.id, m.content, m.sender_id, m.created_at
  FROM messages m
  WHERE m.channel_id = c.id          -- references the outer row
  ORDER BY m.created_at DESC
  LIMIT 1
) lm ON true
```

`ON true` because the join condition already lives inside the subquery. `LEFT` because an empty channel still belongs in the list. And it's fast for the same reason the previous modules were: `idx_messages_channel_created` is `(channel_id, created_at DESC)`, so "newest in this channel" is one index seek per row.

Read receipts, atomically:

```sql
INSERT INTO read_receipts (user_id, channel_id, last_read_message_id, last_read_at)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3, now())
ON CONFLICT (user_id, channel_id)
DO UPDATE SET last_read_message_id = $3, last_read_at = now();
```

Check-then-insert has a race two devices will find within a day: both read "no receipt," both insert, one gets a duplicate-key error you then have to pretend was success.

## In your world

Work through `chat-app-api/LEARNING.md` end to end: junction table and composite primary key for `channel_members`, DM deduplication (two people, one conversation, however many times they tap "message"), the DESC index, `.rpc('get_user_channels')`, and the fire-and-forget notification call in `src/routes/messages.ts` — the pattern you replaced with a real queue in the file vault. Finish with its verification checklist, out loud.

The transferable pattern is the last-message-per-group join. Your work backend needs it anywhere a list shows a summary of its children: the newest comment on a post, the latest activity per group.

## Watch out

- **A lateral join per row is still a query per row** — just without the network. It's fast because of the index. Without `(channel_id, created_at DESC)` it degrades into a sort per channel.
- **Stored functions are code with no code review and no types.** They're invisible to your TypeScript and live only in migrations. Use them where they earn it, and never as the place your business rules quietly accumulate.
- **UPSERT needs a real unique constraint** to conflict on. `ON CONFLICT (user_id, channel_id)` only works because that pair is the primary key.

quiz.q: What can a LATERAL subquery do that a normal subquery cannot?
options: Return more than one row
Reference columns from the outer query, which makes it a per-row 'for each'
Use an index
Be written inside a stored function
quiz.explain: That outer reference is the whole feature: 'for each channel, its newest message' becomes one query plan instead of one query per channel.

quiz.q: Why UPSERT instead of check-then-insert for a read receipt?
options: It sends less data over the wire
It is one atomic statement, so two concurrent requests cannot both decide the row is missing
It skips constraint checks
It avoids needing a primary key
quiz.explain: Check-then-insert is two statements with a gap. Two devices marking read at once both see 'no receipt', both insert, and one gets a duplicate-key error you then have to swallow.

quiz.q: The last-message LATERAL join is fast because of what?
options: The stored function is precompiled
An index on (channel_id, created_at DESC) turns 'newest in this channel' into one seek per row
Postgres caches the subquery result
LATERAL joins are executed in parallel
quiz.explain: Without that index, each lateral iteration sorts the channel's messages. The pattern only pays off when the index matches it.

## The problem

Sharing is where file apps leak. A user shares a folder with a colleague, who can then open every file inside it — including the one moved in yesterday. Now express that as code. Who can read this file: the owner, anyone it was shared with directly, anyone given an ancestor folder, and nobody whose share expired at midnight. Get one branch wrong and it isn't a bug, it's a disclosure.

## The idea

Two ideas carry the whole feature.

**Permissions form a hierarchy, not a set.** `admin > edit > view`. You don't check "does this user have exactly `view`" — you check "does this user hold *any* level that grants `view`." Written as a lookup table instead of a chain of `if`s, that's four lines and no room for a missed case.

**A share points at exactly one thing.** A file, or a folder, never both, never neither. Two nullable columns plus a `CHECK` constraint expresses that in the one place that can't be bypassed: the database. Zod's `.refine()` mirrors the same rule at the API edge so the user gets a 400 instead of a 500, but Zod cannot protect you from a migration, a script, or your own future service code.

## In practice

The hierarchy, and the ordering of the access check:

```ts
const grants: Record<string, string[]> = {
  view: ["view", "edit", "admin"],
  edit: ["edit", "admin"],
  admin: ["admin"],
};
```

Owner first, because the common case should cost zero extra queries; then shares; then expiry. And a share row that has passed `expires_at` is not deleted — it's filtered on read, so revocation and history both work.

The constraint that makes the polymorphic column pair honest:

```sql
CONSTRAINT share_target_check CHECK (
  (file_id IS NOT NULL AND folder_id IS NULL) OR
  (file_id IS NULL AND folder_id IS NOT NULL)
)
```

## In your world

Work through `file-vault-api/LEARNING.md` and finish the build: share routes with `.refine()` cross-field validation, the permission hierarchy in `src/services/share.service.ts`, inherited folder permissions (walk the ancestor chain with the recursive CTE you already have — a share on `/Work` must cover `/Work/Reports/q3.pdf`), and `user_storage_usage` refreshed from the storage-quota job. Then run its verification checklist cold.

What transfers is the check order and the constraint. Your work backend enforces access with row-level security instead of a service function, but the reasoning is identical: put the rule where it cannot be forgotten, and make the cheapest check the first one.

## Watch out

- **Inherited permissions need the ancestor chain, not the immediate parent.** A share on a grandparent folder still grants access, so the check has to walk upward — or you precompute the chain.
- **Expiry must be applied on every read path.** One list endpoint that forgets `expires_at` is a revoked share that still works.
- **`CHECK` is validated on write, not retroactively.** Adding it to a table that already holds bad rows fails the migration, which is good news you'd rather get in dev.

quiz.q: What does the CHECK constraint on the shares table prevent that a zod .refine() cannot?
options: A malformed API request body
Invalid rows written by a migration, a script, or service code that skipped the schema
A missing foreign key target
Two users sharing the same file
quiz.explain: Zod guards the API edge, which is where you want the friendly 400. The constraint guards the data itself, which is the only layer nothing can bypass.

quiz.q: Why does the access check test ownership before looking at shares?
options: Owners have a different permission level
It is the common case and it answers without querying the shares table at all
Shares are stored in a different database
Row-level security requires it
quiz.explain: Cheapest check first. Most reads are by the owner, so the fast path avoids a join and the hierarchy lookup entirely.

quiz.q: A user was granted 'edit' on a folder. What should a 'view' check return?
options: False — the levels do not match exactly
True — edit grants view, because permissions form a hierarchy
True only if a separate view share also exists
It depends on whether the share has expired, and nothing else
quiz.explain: admin implies edit implies view. Expressing that as a lookup table of which levels satisfy a requirement removes the chance of missing a branch.
